cse-2004-cs-47.approach: Average instruction time = CPU time + 2 × (effective memory access time) + (page-fault service time amortised per instruction). Compute the three parts separately.
cse-2004-cs-47.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Memory access | 150 ns |
| Page-fault service | 8 ms |
| CPU time / instruction | 100 ns |
| Memory accesses / instruction | 2 |
| TLB hit ratio | 0.9 |
| Page faults | 1 per 10 000 instructions |

steps.title: Effective memory access time
steps.body:
TLB hit: one access, $150$ ns. On a TLB miss the key's model charges one extra page-table access: $150+150 = 300$ ns.
$$\text{EMAT} = 0.9(150) + 0.1(300) = 135 + 30 = 165\text{ ns}$$

steps.title: Strict two-level check
steps.body: If a TLB miss walks both page-table levels (3 accesses = 450 ns): $\text{EMAT} = 0.9(150)+0.1(450) = 180$ ns, total $100+360+800 = 1260$ ns — not an option. The nearest listed value, and the accepted key, is **1230 ns**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Below the floor 100 + 2×150 + 800 = 1200 ns (CPU + two plain accesses + fault share) — impossible.
Also below the 1200 ns floor, so it undercounts memory or fault time.
1215 ns implies EMAT = 157.5 ns, i.e. only 7.5 ns TLB-miss overhead per access — too little for a 10% miss rate costing ≥ 150 ns each.

pitfalls: Forgetting to amortise the 8 ms fault over 10 000 instructions.
Counting only one memory access per instruction.
cse-2004-cs-47.verification: Recomputed with the strict two-level model (1260 ns, not offered); D is the only option within the plausible 1230–1260 range.

cse-2004-cs-48.approach: Deadlock (circular wait) is impossible if both processes acquire the two semaphores in the same global order. Pick the option where L1,L2 and L3,L4 lock in the same order and never lock the same semaphore twice.

steps.title: Both semaphores are needed
steps.body: Each process updates both X and Y, so each must hold $S_x$ and $S_y$ before the critical section.

steps.title: Same order ⇒ no circular wait
steps.body: With $P_1$: P($S_x$), P($S_y$) and $P_2$: P($S_x$), P($S_y$), whoever gets $S_x$ first also gets $S_y$; the other blocks on $S_x$ while holding nothing. No cycle is possible. The order of the V operations does not matter for deadlock.

steps.title: Check the rest
steps.body: Opposite orders (A, B) allow $P_1$ to hold one semaphore while $P_2$ holds the other ⇒ deadlock. In C, P($S_x$) twice blocks a process on itself.

optionAnalysis.reason: P1 locks Sy then Sx, P2 locks Sx then Sy — opposite orders, circular wait possible.
P1: Sx then Sy, P2: Sy then Sx — opposite orders, deadlock possible.
P(Sx) twice in P1 (and P(Sy) twice in P2): the second P blocks forever on a binary semaphore.
Both acquire Sx before Sy — a global lock order, so no circular wait.

pitfalls: Trying to match the P order to the V order — release order is irrelevant to deadlock.
cse-2004-cs-48.verification: Interleaving check: in D, after P1 takes Sx, P2 blocks at P(Sx) holding nothing; P1 completes and releases both.

cse-2004-cs-49.approach: Count data blocks reachable from the i-node: pointers per block = block size / address size; the triple-indirect term dominates.

steps.title: Bytes
steps.body:
$$2^{24} \times 2^{10} = 2^{34}\text{ bytes (slightly more)}$$
The 48-bit integers (file offsets) allow up to $2^{48}$, and 32-bit block addresses allow $2^{32}$ blocks, so neither is the limiting factor.

optionAnalysis.reason: $2^{24}$ is the number of blocks, not bytes.
$2^{32}$ ignores that each block is $2^{10}$ bytes (or confuses with 32-bit addresses).
$\approx 2^{24}$ blocks × $2^{10}$ bytes = $2^{34}$ bytes.
$2^{48}$ is only the limit of the integer size; the i-node structure caps the file far below it.

pitfalls: Using 48 bits as the pointer size.
Forgetting to multiply blocks by block size.

cse-2004-cs-50.approach: Find the candidate keys, then test BCNF (every determinant a superkey) and 3NF (or RHS prime).

steps.title: Candidate keys
steps.body: courseNo appears on no RHS, so it is in every key. $\{name, courseNo\}^+$ = all attributes (name → rollNo, then grade); likewise $\{rollNo, courseNo\}^+$. Keys: **{name, courseNo}**, **{rollNo, courseNo}**. Prime attributes: name, rollNo, courseNo.

steps.title: BCNF test
steps.body: name → rollNo: name is not a superkey ⇒ **not BCNF**.

steps.title: 3NF test
steps.body: The two grade FDs have key LHS. For name → rollNo and rollNo → name, the RHS is prime. Every FD satisfies 3NF ⇒ highest form is **3NF**.

optionAnalysis.reason: It satisfies 2NF, but also the stronger 3NF.
All FDs either have a key LHS or a prime RHS.
name → rollNo has a non-superkey determinant.
4NF needs BCNF first.

pitfalls: Missing the second candidate key and calling rollNo non-prime (would give 2NF).
cse-2004-cs-50.verification: Closure of {name} alone is {name, rollNo} — not a key, confirming the BCNF violation.

steps.title: The difference
steps.body: All girls minus those girls = girls for whom **no** boy has marks $\ge$ hers, i.e. girls with **more marks than all the boys**.

"More than some boy" would be a plain join result, not a difference.
This describes (roughly) the subtracted part, not the result.

cse-2004-cs-51.verification: Example: boys 50, 70; girls 60, 80 → girl 60 joins boy 70 and is removed; only girl 80 (> all boys) remains.

steps.body: A: $K_A \in \{0,1\}$; B: $K_B \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, all equally likely — $2\times4 = 8$ outcomes.

5 of 8 equally likely pairs.

B can still win (e.g. $K_B=0, K_A=1$).

pitfalls: Forgetting that A's backoff counter resets after its successful transmission.
Counting ties as wins.

cse-2004-cs-56.approach: TCP segment = 180 + 20 = 200 bytes. Network B allows 100 − 20 = 80 bytes of IP payload per fragment (a multiple of 8), so the segment is split into 80 + 80 + 40, each with its own 20-byte IP header; they are not reassembled until the destination.

steps.title: Packet leaving A
steps.body: IP datagram = 20 (IP) + 20 (TCP) + 180 = 220 bytes ≤ 1000, so no fragmentation in A.

steps.title: Entering B (MTU 100)
steps.body: Payload per fragment ≤ $100 - 20 = 80$ bytes (80 is a multiple of 8). The 200-byte IP payload becomes $80 + 80 + 40$ → **3 fragments**.

steps.title: Bytes at destination IP layer
steps.body: Routers do not reassemble, so C receives the 3 fragments: $$(80+20) + (80+20) + (40+20) = 100 + 100 + 60 = 260\text{ bytes}$$

optionAnalysis.reason: 200 bytes is the TCP segment without any IP header.
220 bytes would be the unfragmented datagram — but B forces fragmentation and routers do not reassemble.
240 bytes counts only 2 IP headers; 200 bytes of payload need 3 fragments of ≤ 80.
3 fragments × 20-byte headers + 200 bytes = 260.

pitfalls: Assuming the router into C reassembles the fragments.
Using 100 bytes of payload per fragment (forgetting the IP header).

cse-2004-cs-57.approach: The bottleneck is the 512 Kbps B–C link. Every 180 bytes of application data travel on it as 260 bytes of fragments (Q.56), so the useful-data rate is 512 Kbps × 180/260.

steps.title: Bottleneck link
steps.body: A–B (1 Mbps) carries 220 bytes per message; B–C (512 Kbps) carries 260 bytes per message. Time per message on B–C: $\frac{260\times8}{512\,000}$ s vs. $\frac{220\times8}{10^6}$ s on A–B, so B–C limits the rate.

steps.title: About the stored key
steps.body: 409.6 Kbps $= 512 \times \frac{160}{200}$ does not correspond to the fragment sizes actually sent; with the 260 bytes established in Q.56 the rate is 354.5 Kbps.

answer.keyNote: Stored key C (409.6 Kbps) is an unofficial solved key; with 260 bytes on the 512 Kbps link per 180-byte message the rate is 512 × 180/260 ≈ 354.5 Kbps (B). Flagged needsReview.

optionAnalysis.reason: 325.5 Kbps would mean about 283 bytes on the link per 180-byte message, which matches no fragment/header count.
409.6 = 512 × 0.8 — an 80% efficiency that does not match the 180/260 data fraction on the bottleneck link.
Ignores all header overhead.

pitfalls: Using the unfragmented 220-byte datagram for the B–C link.
Taking the 1 Mbps link as the bottleneck.

cse-2004-cs-62.approach: Add the gate levels along the critical path: generate P, G → two-level carry network → sum XOR. XOR is not an allowed gate, so each XOR costs two levels (AND-OR with complemented inputs available).

steps.title: P and G
steps.body: $G_i = A_iB_i$: 1 level. $P_i = A_i \oplus B_i = A_iB_i' + A_i'B_i$: **2 levels**. Ready at time 2.

steps.title: Carries
steps.body: $C_{i+1} = G_i + P_iG_{i-1} + \dots + P_i\cdots P_0C_0$ as two-level AND-OR: $2 + 2 = 4$.

steps.title: Sum
steps.body: $S_i = P_i \oplus C_i$ needs the complement of $C_i$ too; realised as a two-level AND-OR ($P_iC_i' + P_i'C_i$, the complements being produced in parallel at the same levels): 2 more levels ⇒ $4 + 2 = 6$ time units.

optionAnalysis.reason: 4 is when the carries are ready, before the sum stage.
2 (P) + 2 (carry) + 2 (sum XOR) = 6.
Overcounts — would correspond to ripple-like carry propagation.
Overcounts further.

pitfalls: Counting XOR as a single gate when XOR is not in the allowed set.
